resources.string: Smooth waves that follow the music
Signal shape over time: the bars are PCM, not frequencies. Like vis2 in MusicVis.

Needs the same system permission as the stock visualizer (RECORD_AUDIO). In system mode the microphone stays off: the app reads the player output mix. Android shows the dialog as “Microphone” — that is just the permission name.
Visualizer allowed. Play some music and set the wallpaper.
Ready-made palettes. “Original (ice)” is the dark blue / violet gradient from MusicVis vis3.
Frequencies left to right (low → high), like vis3 in MusicVis.
Play music and enable “Beat haptics”. The pulse fires only on the kick attack (~40–130 Hz), not on overall loudness. The slider is a motor test.
Logarithmic frequency scale, like an equalizer: more room for the bass.
Spectrogram: fresh sound on top, time flows down.
Analog level needle with a peak lamp, like vis4.
A swarm of dots: waves recede into the depth, like vis5.
Raw wave as a thin line on a grid, like an oscilloscope screen.
Frequencies around a circle, the core breathes with loudness.
OriginOS 6: icon colors from the palette, 120 Hz, parallax, tilt, cutout, widget, track from the player.
Everything here works on top of any wallpaper mode and applies instantly. Flash and rings follow the kick drum.
Turns on all the effects at once and boosts the bars. For the table at a party, not for battery life.
The whole screen is a color lamp: bass, mids and highs light their own zones.
The screen works as a party lamp: bass lights the bottom of the screen, mids the center, highs the top, and a white core pulses with loudness. Best seen from across the room.

All modes read the same audio. By default it is the phone’s output mix (whatever is playing) captured exactly like the stock Android visualizer — the microphone stays off. In Settings you can switch to the microphone: then the wallpaper reacts to any sound around you, and the picture no longer depends on the media volume.

Modes in the first group scale with the media volume (louder music — bigger picture; the response is boosted at quiet levels). Modes in the second group use normalized frequency data and look the same at any volume.

The palette from “Bar colors” applies to every mode.
Smoothed waveform: the audio wave drawn as soft flowing curves. Works on the raw signal (PCM) and reacts to volume.
The classic vis2 from Android MusicVis: the bars show the raw waveform (PCM) over time — the shape of the signal, not its frequencies.
The raw wave as a thin bright line with a soft glow on a grid — like a lab oscilloscope. PCM.
Waveform history as a swarm of dots: each new wave row pushes the older ones into the distance, where they fade out.
An analog needle shows loudness (RMS): fast attack, slow release, plus a peak lamp — like on tape decks. Like vis4.
Frequency bars arranged around a circle; the inner core pulses with overall loudness. FFT + RMS.
A true frequency histogram (FFT): low frequencies on the left, high on the right. Rendered with OpenGL at up to 120 Hz. Like vis3.
The same FFT on a logarithmic frequency scale, like an equalizer: the bass gets more room, the highs are compressed. OpenGL.
A spectrogram: every row is one FFT snapshot — fresh sound at the top, time flows down. Color shows energy.
